title: Two entries disagree about the same thing
when: Two entries in a client's history record conflicting facts about the same kind of event (for example two different preferred channels).
steps: Agent 14 (CRM & Pipeline) keeps both entries.
It flags the second as conflicting, naming the field.
never: Merge, overwrite or pick between conflicting entries.
why: The history is evidence. Deciding which fact is true is a person's job, with both in view.
you_see: Both entries in the history, the second flagged.
test: A client asks to be texted, then minutes later to be emailed. Both changes are recorded; the second is flagged on the channel field.

title: Two records might be the same person
when: A new inquiry shares a phone number with an existing client but the name differs.
steps: Nothing is merged.
The new inquiry is held and you are asked to continue (a separate person) or cancel.
why: A wrong merge mixes two people's private information and consent.
you_see: A held inquiry naming the possible match.
test: "Avery Synth" and later "A. Synthe" with the same phone number.

title: A report covers a period with a gap in the record
when: A report is produced for a time when some entries could not be written.
steps: The report names the gap and the client it affects.
It never smooths over missing entries.
never: Produce a report that hides a logging gap.
why: A report that looks complete when it is not leads to wrong decisions.
you_see: The end-of-day report listing the logging gap.
test: A client's record is frozen (a deletion request) before the lead's entries arrive, so they are refused; the end-of-day report names that client as a logging gap.

title: A client's consent conflicts across channels
when: A client opted out of a channel and later says something that sounds like yes to it.
steps: The most restrictive answer stands on each channel.
A later yes does not lift a no on its own; only a consent record you sign, marked as reconfirmed by the client, does.
Nothing confirming the change is sent to the client; you are told the opt-out stands.
never: Lift an opt-out because the client seemed to change their mind in passing.
why: Contact rules require clear consent. Your signed record of the client's reconfirmation is that proof.
you_see: A question saying the opt-out stands until a reconfirmed consent record is signed.
test: A lead says no to texts at capture; the next day writes "Please text me from now on". Texts stay no and no confirmation is sent.

title: Someone asks to delete a client's record
when: A request to delete a client's record arrives.
steps: Agent 14 deletes nothing.
It raises a legal-line alert for you.
never: Delete a record on its own.
why: Retention periods are set by law in your state, not by judgment.
you_see: A legal-line alert about the deletion request.
test: A signed request to delete a lead's record.

title: Two records look like the same person
when: Two inquiries match on name and phone (written differently).
steps: Agent 14 proposes the match with the evidence.
You decide: continue keeps them as separate people; nothing is merged automatically.
why: Even a strong match can be two people (a parent and child at one number). A person confirms.
you_see: A held inquiry naming the possible match and what continue means.

title: A change would overwrite history
when: A fact in a client's history changes.
steps: The change is added as a new entry.
The old entry stays; nothing is edited or erased.
why: The history is written in ink: it shows what was true when, which is what protects you in a dispute.
test: You sign email consent "yes", then "no". Both are recorded as separate entries.

title: Imported data conflicts with the record
when: Data imported from another system disagrees with the record.
steps: The record wins.
The import's differences are flagged.
never: Let an import overwrite the record.
why: The record is built from signed and logged events; an import is someone else's copy.

title: An agent asks for a client record it has no route to
when: An agent asks the CRM for a client's record without a route that allows it.
steps: The dispatcher refuses the request before Agent 14 sees it.
never: Share a client's record with an agent that has no need to know.
why: Need-to-know is built into the routes; it does not depend on anyone's judgment.
test: Agent 06 asks for a client's record; only Agents 01, 11, 13 and 15 may. Stand-in: the test sends it as Agent 06.

title: A deletion request freezes the record
when: A retention or deletion request arrives for a client.
steps: Agent 14 freezes the record: nothing is deleted and nothing new is written.
It raises a legal-line alert for you.
Any later attempt to write to the frozen record is refused and you are told.
never: Decide a deletion on its own.
why: Deletion is the owner's decision under the law. Freezing keeps everything as it was until you decide.
you_see: A legal-line alert; questions when something tries to write to the frozen record.
test: A signed deletion request for a lead; the next day the client asks to be texted. The write to the record is refused. (The confirmation of the channel change still goes to the client.)

title: You record who has access to a property
when: You sign an access grant (for example an inspector's access).
steps: Agent 14 records only the party, the end of the access window and a custody reference.
It rejects the whole grant if it has any other field, or if a value looks like the code itself.
never: Store an access code in the record.
why: A code in the record is a code anyone with record access can read.
you_see: A rejection for a grant with a code in it; the clean grant kept.
test: Three signed grants: one with "lockbox code 4411" as the reference (rejected), one with an extra code field (rejected), one clean (kept).

title: An access window has ended and is still open
when: An access window's end date has passed and you have not closed it.
steps: Agent 14 flags it to you once.
It does not repeat the flag every day.
why: You need to know access is still open; a daily repeat trains people to ignore it.
you_see: One question saying the access window has ended.
test: An inspector's access ends October 16; the daily clock runs on the 17th and 18th. One flag.

title: A record cannot be filed in the client's drawer
when: Filing a record in the client's document drawer fails.
steps: The refusal is recorded and held for you.
The CRM entry still stands, and the work goes on.
never: Lose the entry, or hide that filing failed.
why: The drawer is the client's file; you need to know when something is missing from it.
you_see: A question saying the drawer filing was refused.
test: A lead comes in under the client name "Jane Synth"; a space is not allowed in a drawer folder name, so filing is refused, and the lead is still captured.

title: You sign a client's consent record
when: You sign a consent record for a client.
steps: Each channel is set as signed.
A channel the client opted out of stays "no" unless the record says the client reconfirmed it.
A record that cannot be read is rejected whole.
never: Turn an opt-out back on without the client's reconfirmation.
why: Consent is the client's. Your signature records it; it cannot override their opt-out without their word.
you_see: Questions when a channel stays "no" or a record is rejected.
test: A lead opted out of texts. You sign text and email "yes": text stays no. You sign text "maybe": rejected. You sign text "yes" marked reconfirmed by the client: text becomes yes.
